questions: Explain the ordinary environmental-air exhaust separation rule in the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code and the conditions that can change intake separation. Keep other exhaust classes distinct.

For this hypothetical, an exhaust and intake serve the same dwelling, the exhaust is Class 2 at exactly four hundred cfm, and cross contamination plus re-entrainment is five percent. Does that qualify for the intake-separation exception on those facts?
checks:

Environmental-air exhaust outlets are not classified as hazardous or noxious under that item.

The stated exception removes the 10-foot mechanical-intake separation only for the qualifying same-space arrangement: less than 750 cfm of Class 1 exhaust serving a single room, dwelling unit, or sleeping unit; or less than 400 cfm of Class 2 exhaust serving a single dwelling unit or sleeping unit. For either alternative, the combined energy-recovery-device cross contamination and exhaust re-entrainment through the intake must be less than 10 percent of intake airflow, as established by the manufacturer. The flow, served-space, and contamination conditions all matter. The exception does not waive the property-line or operable-opening separations. Air Class is determined under ASHRAE 62.1, not by inventing a classification from this section.

Item 1 addresses the separately specified noxious, toxic, explosive, or flammable exhaust category; item 2 addresses other product-conveying outlets. Their different distances are not the ordinary environmental-air rule. Discharge from a non-evaporative heat-rejection or heat-absorption appliance is not exhaust for the stated rule and has no intake-separation requirement of its own, but its inlet/discharge must not reduce required separation between other exhausts and intakes.

Item 6 additionally addresses individual dwelling-unit exhaust in R-2 and R-3. questions: Explain the current NYC Fire Code fire-protection and security requirements for temporarily unoccupied premises, including tenant spaces. Keep unsafe-building status separate.
A tenant space is temporarily unoccupied, with no commissioner authorization to disable protection. Does vacancy itself allow its sprinkler system to be turned off?

Under FC 311.1, a vacant building, structure, premises, or part is treated as temporarily unoccupied. A separate direction applies when premises have been deemed unsafe under Title 28 Article 216: safeguarding and maintenance must follow the applicable DOB and/or HPD requirements. Unsafe status and temporary unoccupancy are not synonyms.

The temporary-unoccupancy provisions expressly include tenant spaces. Exterior and interior openings accessible to unauthorized persons, including tenants, must be locked or otherwise protected against unauthorized entry. Fire alarm, sprinkler, and standpipe systems must remain operable at all times unless the commissioner authorizes otherwise. Rated partitions, barriers, and walls—including separations around temporarily unoccupied tenant spaces—must be maintained; their openings, joints, and penetrations must be protected under Building Code Chapter 7.

Owners must regularly remove rubbish and combustible waste and prevent new accumulation. The stated construction/repair exception is limited to work complying with the Building Code and waste controlled and removed under FC 304; it is not a general permission to accumulate debris.

FC 311.4 distinguishes facility-closure requirements for unsafe vacant premises containing hazardous materials from those for temporarily unoccupied premises containing materials regulated by FC Chapter 50. It also requires premises thereafter to remain free of hazardous materials except as approved by the commissioner. Those separate triggers should not be merged.

Unoccupied tenant spaces in covered malls have additional conditions: no combustible-material storage, maintained fire separation, inspection at least weekly, secured doors, and no rubbish or other combustible waste.
